analysis.one_liner: Adds a capped Medicare benefit covering up to 20 hours a week of in-home help with daily living.
analysis.headline: The Medicare at Home Act was introduced in the Senate with no cosponsors and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds a new Medicare benefit paying for a home care worker to help older and disabled people with everyday tasks — bathing, dressing, meals, medication reminders — for up to 20 hours a week. To qualify, a doctor must certify the person needs help with at least two daily activities. It would be paid for by adjusting Medicare Part B monthly premiums, with the Chief Actuary required to report the premium impact within 180 days.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who need help with daily activities — bathing, dressing, eating — and the family members who currently provide or pay for that care, which the bill's findings say can exceed $60,000 a year out of pocket or force people to spend down into Medicaid. Home care workers also gain from a required wage floor and 20-hours-per-week billing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Older and disabled people needing home care

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Medicare benefit covering up to 20 hours per week of help at home with daily activities like bathing, dressing, and eating, for people who need help with at least two such activities.
Reduces the need to spend down into Medicaid or pay out of pocket, which the bill's findings say can exceed $60,000 a year.
Directs HHS to set a reasonable wage floor for home care workers under the payment methodology, and sets standards for worker qualifications and agency enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries, through higher Part B premiums adjusted to cover the benefit's additional actuarial cost under the standard premium subsidy schedule; the bill also leaves workers' qualification standards and payment rates to later regulation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare beneficiaries via Part B premiums

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by adjusting the monthly Medicare Part B premium to cover the benefit's full additional actuarial cost, so beneficiaries would pay for much of the new benefit through higher premiums, and the bill does not estimate that amount up front.

The benefit is capped at 20 hours per week, which will not cover the needs of people requiring round-the-clock or near-continuous care, and requires a physician-certified plan showing need for help with at least two daily activities, which adds an administrative gate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and popular, but it is not free: the bill pays for it by raising Medicare Part B premiums, so beneficiaries (including those who never need home care) would bear much of the cost through higher monthly premiums, on top of any government contribution. The 20-hour weekly cap and the certification requirement limit both the help and the cost. As written, the bill leaves the actual premium increase to be determined later by the actuary, so the size of the burden is unknown.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, but with no cosponsors it never got a hearing or a vote and will likely die there when this Congress ends in January 2027.

narrative.text: The Senate introduced the bill on August 5, 2026, and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral is the only action since.
No senators have cosponsored the bill, according to the Congress.gov cosponsor list.
The bill would amend Medicare to add home care services — help with bathing, dressing, meals, and similar needs — as a Part B benefit capped at 20 hours per week.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the outcome so far; the bill simply sits in committee, preserving the status quo in which families pay out of pocket or rely on Medicaid.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo: no one moved it forward

for.name: Sen. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare at Home Act and got it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition has emerged yet.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and home care workers
industries.note: The bill creates a new paid, Medicare-reimbursed market for home care and requires a wage floor for workers, potentially raising pay in a low-wage field. Agencies gain a large new customer base.
Beneficiaries gain a new benefit but pay for its additional actuarial cost through higher Part B premiums under the standard subsidy schedule.

industries.industry: Medicaid home- and community-based care programs
industries.note: People already receiving comparable Medicaid home care are excluded from the new benefit, so state programs remain the channel for the highest-need populations; some pressure to shift to Medicare could grow over time.

analysis.trajectory: Bills introduced this late in a two-year Congress with zero cosponsors and a single referral rarely move; unless Senator Kim attracts cosponsors and the Finance Committee schedules action, the bill will expire when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
